title: 2 Samuel 3:6–21
context: As the war continues, Abner, the commander who had made Ishbosheth king, has become the real power in Saul’s house. When Ishbosheth accuses him of going in to Rizpah, Saul’s concubine, Abner reacts with fury and swears to transfer the kingdom to David, invoking what the LORD has sworn to David. Ishbosheth is too afraid to answer. Abner opens negotiations, and David demands as a condition the return of his wife Michal, Saul’s daughter, who is taken from her weeping husband Paltiel. Abner then persuades the elders of Israel and the men of Benjamin, appealing to the LORD’s word about David, and comes to Hebron with twenty men. David holds a feast for them and sends Abner away in peace to gather all Israel. Both traditions read this as a passage in which God’s stated purpose for David advances through mixed and self-interested human motives.

verses.text: While there was war between Saul’s house and David’s house, Abner made himself strong in Saul’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that Abner is described as making himself strong in Saul’s house, a phrase that points to his own ambition and initiative. The narrator presents him as a capable man pursuing his own position, and his choices will shape the course of events in significant ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that while Abner strengthens his hold on Saul’s house, the larger movement of the chapter is already set by verse 1, where Saul’s house is weakening. Both traditions agree that human power-building is real, yet it operates within a story in which God’s purpose for David is moving forward.

verses.text: Now Saul had a concubine, whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah; and Ishbosheth said to Abner, “Why have you gone in to my father’s concubine?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that Ishbosheth’s accusation concerns Rizpah, Saul’s concubine. In the ancient world, taking a former king’s concubine could be read as a claim to the throne, so the charge may be political as well as moral, though the text does not say whether the accusation was true.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the political weight of the charge and the uncertainty about whether Abner was guilty. Both traditions observe that the narrator leaves the question open and focuses instead on how the confrontation exposes the weakness of Ishbosheth and the real power held by Abner.

verses.text: Then Abner was very angry about Ishbosheth’s words, and said, “Am I a dog’s head that belongs to Judah? Today I show kindness to your father Saul’s house, to his brothers, and to his friends, and have not delivered you into the hand of David; and yet you charge me today with a fault concerning this woman!
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Abner’s angry response stresses his loyalty to Saul’s house and the favors he has shown. His question about being a dog’s head expresses wounded pride. The passage shows how personal resentment can become the hinge on which political loyalties turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Abner frames himself as Saul’s house’s protector, claiming he has not delivered Ishbosheth into David’s hand. Both traditions see the irony that a man defending his own honor is about to become the agent who hands the kingdom to David, which shows how God can use even offended pride.

verses.text: God do so to Abner, and more also, if, as the LORD has sworn to David, I don’t do even so to him:
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Abner swears an oath invoking what the LORD has sworn to David. This shows that the LORD’s purpose for David was known, yet Abner had fought against it until now; his change of course seems driven by anger as much as conviction, so his acknowledgment of God’s word comes late and with mixed motives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in Abner’s words an admission that the LORD’s oath to David stood all along, even while Abner opposed it. Both traditions agree that knowing God’s purpose and aligning oneself with it are different things, and that God’s word here proves sure regardless of when or why Abner submits to it.

verses.text: to transfer the kingdom from Saul’s house, and to set up David’s throne over Israel and over Judah, from Dan even to Beersheba.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that Abner announces his plan to transfer the kingdom and set up David’s throne over Israel and Judah from Dan to Beersheba, a phrase for the whole land. Abner speaks as though the transfer depends on him, and humanly he does hold real influence over its timing and manner.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the kingdom Abner promises to deliver is the one God had already given to David by anointing. Both traditions affirm that God works through human agents like Abner, and that Abner’s actions, though genuinely his, serve to bring about the unified kingdom God intended.

verses.text: He could not answer Abner another word, because he was afraid of him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Ishbosheth cannot answer because he is afraid of Abner. His fear shows how dependent he is on the commander who made him king, and his silence marks a failure of leadership that leaves his throne exposed and his followers without direction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the scene shows the hollowness of a throne that rested on Abner’s strength rather than on God’s appointment. Both traditions agree that the narrator is showing why Saul’s house collapses: its king lacks both divine sanction and personal authority.

verses.text: Abner sent messengers to David on his behalf, saying, “Whose is the land?” and saying, “Make your alliance with me, and behold, my hand will be with you to bring all Israel around to you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that Abner’s message, asking whose the land is, can be read as either acknowledging David’s claim or emphasizing Abner’s own power to deliver it; the question is ambiguous. He offers a covenant and promises to bring all Israel around to David, taking initiative in the negotiation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the ambiguity of Abner’s question and his evident bargaining for advantage. Both traditions observe that the alliance is a political deal, and that God’s purpose for David is being served through negotiation and self-interest rather than through pure devotion.

verses.text: David said, “Good. I will make a treaty with you, but one thing I require of you. That is, you will not see my face unless you first bring Michal, Saul’s daughter, when you come to see my face.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that David agrees to a treaty but makes the return of Michal a condition. Michal had been given to David by Saul and later given to another man (1 Samuel 18:27; 25:44). David’s demand restores his claim, and it may also strengthen his link to Saul’s house in the eyes of the northern tribes, though the text gives no motive.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also observe that reclaiming Michal may carry political significance, linking David to Saul’s family as he moves to rule all Israel. Both traditions recognize that David’s motives are not spelled out, and both read the demand soberly, since it will bring real grief to Michal’s second husband.

verses.text: David sent messengers to Ishbosheth, Saul’s son, saying, “Deliver me my wife Michal, whom I was given to marry for one hundred foreskins of the Philistines.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that David sends his request directly to Ishbosheth, recalling that Michal was given to him for one hundred Philistine foreskins (1 Samuel 18:25–27). By appealing to the original agreement, David presents the demand as a matter of a legitimate prior claim rather than simple force.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that David’s message addresses Ishbosheth formally, as Saul’s son, while Abner is the one actually managing affairs. Both traditions see David acting carefully and lawfully in public, grounding his claim in an earlier covenant rather than seizing what he wants.

verses.text: Ishbosheth sent and took her from her husband, Paltiel the son of Laish.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that Ishbosheth complies and takes Michal from Paltiel the son of Laish. The weak king’s compliance shows how little room he has to resist, and the narrative quietly notes that a woman is moved between men by political decisions in which she is given no voice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that Michal is treated as a pawn in a political settlement, and the text does not hide the cost. Both traditions agree that Scripture records such events honestly without approving everything in them, and that the human costs of power struggles are part of the story.

verses.text: Her husband went with her, weeping as he went, and followed her to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, “Go! Return!” and he returned.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers are struck by Paltiel weeping as he follows Michal to Bahurim until Abner sends him back. The brief scene gives a human face to the cost of David’s demand, and invites readers to feel the real grief caused by decisions made for political advantage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also find the scene of Paltiel’s grief deeply poignant and see the narrator deliberately preserving it. Both traditions agree that the account of David’s rise does not hide the wounds it causes, and that God’s purposes advancing through history do not erase the suffering of ordinary people along the way.

verses.text: Abner had communication with the elders of Israel, saying, “In times past, you sought for David to be king over you.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Abner reminds the elders of Israel that they had already wanted David as king. This suggests real support for David among the northern tribes, which Abner now harnesses, and it shows that the people’s own desires and choices are part of how the kingdom comes together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Abner frames the elders’ earlier desire as something now ready to be fulfilled. Both traditions agree that the movement toward David’s kingship involves genuine human consent, as the elders of Israel are persuaded rather than coerced into accepting him.

verses.text: Now then do it! For the LORD has spoken of David, saying, ‘By the hand of my servant David, I will save my people Israel out of the hand of the Philistines, and out of the hand of all their enemies.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Abner appeals to the LORD’s word that by the hand of his servant David he would save Israel from the Philistines and from all their enemies. Abner uses God’s promise to persuade, calling the elders to act on what they know and respond to God’s stated purpose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in this verse an emphasis on God’s own declaration about David, which stands behind all the political maneuvering. Both traditions agree that the promise is God’s and that David’s calling is to save God’s people, and Abner’s appeal gathers up what the earlier chapters have shown in David’s anointing and his victories over the Philistines (1 Samuel 16:13; 1 Samuel 17).

verses.text: Abner also spoke in the ears of Benjamin; and Abner went also to speak in the ears of David in Hebron all that seemed good to Israel and to the whole house of Benjamin.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that Abner speaks directly to Benjamin, Saul’s own tribe, whose support would be most difficult to win. His careful diplomacy shows the importance of persuasion and consent among the tribes, and the narrative treats the gaining of their loyalty as a real achievement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Benjamin’s inclusion is significant because it shows even Saul’s tribe moving toward David. Both traditions see Abner’s diplomacy as the means by which the whole of Israel, including those closest to Saul, is drawn toward the king God had chosen.

verses.text: So Abner came to David to Hebron, and twenty men with him. David made Abner and the men who were with him a feast.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that Abner comes to Hebron with twenty men, and David hosts a feast for them. The feast likely seals the alliance in a public and hospitable way, and David’s generosity signals goodwill toward his former enemy, which the narrative presents as wise and gracious conduct.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that David’s feast reflects his patience and willingness to receive former opponents. Both traditions agree that David’s conduct here is marked by restraint and openness, which contrasts sharply with the violence Joab is about to commit.

verses.text: Abner said to David, “I will arise and go, and will gather all Israel to my lord the king, that they may make a covenant with you, and that you may reign over all that your soul desires.” David sent Abner away; and he went in peace.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Abner pledges to gather all Israel so that they may make a covenant with David, and David sends him away in peace. The repeated phrase about going in peace stresses that David’s intentions toward Abner were peaceful, which matters for what follows.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the emphasis on peace, which the narrator repeats in the following verses to make David’s innocence clear. Both traditions agree that the covenant Abner proposes would unite the kingdom under David and that the narrator is setting up the tragic contrast of Joab’s actions.
